hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: In a Mercator-style URL frontier, what roles do the 'front' queues and 'back' queues play?
options: Front queues store fetched HTML, and back queues store parsed links
Front queues order URLs by priority, and each back queue holds URLs for a single host so politeness delays can be enforced per host
Front queues handle DNS, and back queues handle robots.txt
Front queues are in memory, and back queues are an on-disk copy of the same data
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: Front queues decide what to crawl next (importance, freshness). A selector moves URLs into per-host back queues, and a heap keyed by each host's next allowed fetch time decides which host a worker may hit. That separates prioritization from politeness.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: Which behavior best defines crawler politeness?
options: Fetching as many pages per second from each site as bandwidth allows
Sending a custom User-Agent and nothing else
Limiting concurrency and request rate per host (e.g. one connection, with a delay between fetches) and honoring robots.txt
Only crawling sites that have a sitemap
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: A crawler can easily overload a small site, so it caps per-host load and respects robots.txt rules (and a Crawl-delay where supported). A User-Agent identifies you but doesn't limit load, and sitemaps are optional hints.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: A crawler uses a Bloom filter of seen URLs to skip duplicates across billions of URLs. What is the consequence of a false positive?
options: A never-seen URL is wrongly treated as seen and skipped
An already-crawled URL is fetched again
The filter crashes and must be rebuilt
Two different URLs get merged into one page
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: Bloom filters never give false negatives but can give false positives. So the risk is missing some new pages, not re-crawling old ones. You size the filter (bits per element, hash count) to keep that rate acceptably low, e.g. about 1%.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: Many URLs serve nearly identical pages that differ only in an ad block or timestamp. Which technique detects such near-duplicates?
options: Comparing full SHA-256 hashes of the HTML
Comparing URL lengths
Comparing HTTP status codes
Locality-sensitive fingerprints such as SimHash, where similar documents have fingerprints differing in only a few bits
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: A cryptographic hash changes completely if one byte differs, so it only catches exact duplicates. SimHash or MinHash map similar content to nearby fingerprints, allowing a Hamming-distance check. Google has described using SimHash for near-duplicate detection in web crawling.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: Which of these is a sensible URL normalization step before deduplication?
options: Lowercase the scheme and host, drop default ports and #fragments, and sort query parameters where safe
Lowercase the entire URL, including the path
Remove every query parameter from every URL
Convert https URLs to http
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: Scheme and host are case-insensitive, default ports and fragments don't change the resource, and parameter order usually doesn't either. Paths can be case-sensitive, and stripping all query parameters would merge genuinely different pages (e.g. ?id=1 vs ?id=2).

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: A crawler gets stuck on a site whose calendar page links to 'next month' forever, generating endless unique URLs. What is the standard defense against such spider traps?
options: Increase the Bloom filter size
Cap crawl depth, URL length and pages per host, and flag hosts with abnormal URL growth
Only crawl pages with fewer than 10 links
Retry the site later with more workers
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: Each trap URL is genuinely new, so dedup doesn't help. Per-host budgets, depth and length limits and pattern detection stop the crawler wasting resources. A bigger filter only remembers more trap URLs, and more workers make it worse.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: A crawler must fetch 1 billion pages per month. Roughly what average fetch rate is that?
options: About 40 pages/s
About 4,000 pages/s
About 390 pages/s
About 40,000 pages/s
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: A 30-day month is 30 × 86,400 ≈ 2.6 million seconds, and 1,000,000,000 / 2,592,000 ≈ 386 pages/s. Plan for about 2x that at peak. At ~100 KB per page this is roughly 40 MB/s of download, and about 100 TB of raw HTML per month.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: Which practices are correct for handling robots.txt? Select all that apply.
options: Cache each host's robots.txt and refresh it periodically (e.g. daily)
Apply the rules for the group matching your crawler's user-agent, falling back to the `*` group
Fetch robots.txt once ever per host and never refresh it
Treat robots.txt as access control that stops anyone else from fetching those pages
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: RFC 9309 has crawlers pick the most specific user-agent group and allows caching (generally no longer than 24 hours). Sites change their rules, so never refreshing is wrong. robots.txt is a voluntary convention, not security, and real access control needs authentication.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: Which properties of a standard Bloom filter are true? Select all that apply.
options: It never returns false negatives for inserted items
Its false-positive rate rises as more items are added beyond its design capacity
Standard Bloom filters can't delete items
It answers membership exactly with no errors
Its memory grows with the length of each inserted URL
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: Inserted items always test positive, filling the bit array raises false positives, and clearing bits could erase other items (counting Bloom filters work around that). Memory is a fixed bit array regardless of key length, and membership is probabilistic.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: Partitioning the frontier by a hash of the hostname makes politeness easier, because one worker owns all URLs for a given host.
options: True
False
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: True. Host-based partitioning means one place controls each host's request rate with no cross-worker coordination, and per-host state (robots.txt, DNS) stays local. Partitioning by full-URL hash would spread one host across many workers.

hld-crawler-dropbox:0.prompt: A crawler should recrawl every page at the same frequency so that all sites are treated fairly.
options: True
False
hld-crawler-dropbox:0.explanation: False. Pages change at very different rates: news front pages change every few minutes, archived pages almost never. Recrawl schedules should adapt to observed change frequency and importance, often using conditional GETs (If-Modified-Since, ETag) to save bandwidth.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: Why does a Dropbox-like sync client split files into blocks (Dropbox has described 4 MB blocks) instead of uploading whole files?
options: Object storage can't store files over 4 MB
Blocks are encrypted, while whole files can't be
Blocks make files load faster in the web preview
Only changed blocks need uploading, uploads can resume per block, and identical blocks can be deduplicated
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: Editing part of a 2 GB file re-uploads only the blocks that changed, a failed upload resumes at the block level, and content-hashed blocks are stored once. Storage limits and encryption aren't the reason; whole files can be encrypted too.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: With fixed-size chunking, a user inserts one byte at the start of a large file and almost every block changes. What fixes this?
options: Content-defined chunking (e.g. a Rabin rolling hash) that picks boundaries from the content, so boundaries after the edit realign
Making blocks smaller
Compressing each block before hashing
Hashing the file name instead of the content
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: Fixed offsets shift after an insertion, so every later block's hash changes. Content-defined chunking sets a boundary wherever a rolling hash matches a pattern, so after the edited region boundaries fall on the same content and later blocks dedupe again (as in rsync, restic and LBFS). Smaller fixed blocks still shift.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: How does block-level deduplication work in a file sync service?
options: Files with the same name are stored once
Each block is stored under its cryptographic content hash, so a block already stored is never stored again
Duplicate files are zipped together nightly
Users are asked to delete duplicates manually
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: Content addressing (e.g. SHA-256 per block) means identical bytes give an identical key, so a second copy only adds a reference. Names say nothing about content: two files can share a name and differ, or differ in name and be identical.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: In a Dropbox-style design, how are metadata and file contents stored?
options: Both in one relational table, with file bytes in a BLOB column
Both on the user's device only
A metadata service maps each file path and version to an ordered list of block hashes, while a separate block store holds the immutable blocks
Metadata in object storage and blocks in the SQL database
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: Metadata is small, relational and updated transactionally, while blocks are large, immutable and content-addressed. Splitting them lets each scale independently. Dropbox built Magic Pocket for blocks and keeps metadata in its own database systems. BLOBs in SQL scale poorly at exabyte size.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: How should a desktop client learn promptly that files changed on another device, without hammering the server?
options: Poll the full file listing every 5 seconds
Re-download every file hourly
Have the server email the client
Hold a long-poll (or push) connection that signals 'something changed', then fetch only the delta since the client's cursor
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: A cheap notification channel plus cursor-based delta fetching keeps traffic proportional to changes. Dropbox's public API exposes this pattern as list_folder/longpoll plus list_folder/continue with a cursor. Full listings every few seconds waste huge amounts of work for idle accounts.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: Two offline laptops both edit report.docx and then reconnect. Dropbox's documented behavior is to:
options: Keep one version and save the other as a separate 'conflicted copy' file
Merge the two Word documents automatically line by line
Keep whichever save has the later device clock timestamp and discard the other
Reject the second upload and lose its changes
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: For opaque binary files there's no safe automatic merge, so Dropbox preserves both: one keeps the name and the other becomes '... (conflicted copy)'. Last-writer-wins by device clock would silently lose work, and clocks can be skewed.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: Before uploading a modified file, the client sends the server the list of its block hashes. Why?
options: To let the server verify the user's password
So the server can reply with only the hashes it doesn't already have, and the client uploads just those blocks
To reserve storage quota for the whole file
Because HTTP requires a manifest before a body
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: This 'have/need' exchange skips blocks that already exist from earlier versions or (with cross-user dedup) other users, saving bandwidth. The metadata commit then references the full block list. Authentication and quota are handled separately.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: Which are real risks or costs of deduplicating blocks across different users? Select all that apply.
options: A side channel: an attacker can infer whether a file exists elsewhere by seeing if an upload is skipped
Deleting data safely requires reference counting or garbage collection across users
It complicates per-user encryption, since identical plaintext must map to an identical stored block
It increases total storage used
It makes uploads of popular files slower
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: Instant 'upload complete' responses can leak existence, which is why many services dedupe only within a user or on the server side. Shared blocks need refcounts before deletion, and per-user keys conflict with global dedup. Dedup saves storage and speeds up uploads.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: Which fields belong in a file's metadata record in a block-based sync system? Select all that apply.
options: The file path within the user's namespace
A version or revision identifier
The ordered list of block hashes making up the content
The file's raw bytes
A copy of every other user's file list
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: Path, revision and block list let any client reconstruct the file by fetching blocks from the block store. Raw bytes belong in the block store, and other users' listings have no place in one user's metadata.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: When one user deletes a file, its blocks can be removed from the block store as soon as the file disappears from that user's namespace.
options: True
False
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: False. Deduplicated blocks may be referenced by other files, older versions kept for history or restore, or other users. Blocks must be reference-counted or garbage-collected after a retention window, never deleted eagerly.

hld-crawler-dropbox:1.prompt: Magic Pocket is Dropbox's in-house block storage system, which it built to move most user file data off Amazon S3.
options: True
False
hld-crawler-dropbox:1.explanation: True. Dropbox announced in 2016 that it had migrated the vast majority of user data from S3 to Magic Pocket, its own exabyte-scale, erasure-coded block store, to cut costs and gain control over performance.
